sections.name: Top stories
sections.label: Top stories
sections.glance: GPT-6.2 Astra second on the index at a seventh of the leader's cost per task, a machine-checked Riemann Hypothesis proof, Anthropic's IPO, a licence for every AI data centre that may serve Chinese firms, and canary prompts inside inference providers.
sections.lead: Five stories. Two are about what models can now do and what that costs: OpenAI's new frontier model closed most of the gap to the leader at a fraction of the cost per task, and a Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis made with Claude passed every machine check while mathematicians had yet to understand it. Two are about money and access: the lab behind the leading model went public, and the US made remote access to AI chips a licensed export. The last is security: planted prompts showed that a zero-retention flag does not protect a prompt from an attacker already inside the provider.

sections.name: Models & releases
sections.label: Models
sections.glance: Gemini 4 Neon, the boards compressing at the top, Inkling 2 Mini's looped MoE, Microsoft's seven MAI models, Hy4 Flash's weights, a router atop Terminal-Bench 4.1, a harness study and the retirements on the calendar. Holds the cost chart.
sections.lead: The week's releases made the top of the boards crowded and the bottom of the price list cheap. Google's Neon landed one point behind GPT-6.2 Astra; on Vals the top five are within 1.2 points, so cost per task, not score, separates them. Below that, open weights kept arriving with unusual designs (a looped MoE that fits a laptop, a model with 64B parameters of n-gram tables), and two measurement items said the same thing from different sides: a router can top a leaderboard, and the harness can change a model's cost several times over.

sections.name: Research & papers
sections.label: Research
sections.glance: A rollout cap that becomes a learned limit (this week's paper page), the sampler behind high-temperature collapse, weight-space programming's first week of papers, Physics of LMs 4.2, blind sparse-attention heads, hackable verifiers, and lab-reported results. Holds the sampler animation.
sections.lead: Several of the week's papers found a failure in a knob everyone treats as harmless. A training-time rollout cap taught small models to stop thinking early; a sampler, not the model, explained why generations fall apart at high temperature; a few heads, not the sparsity budget, explained why sparse attention misses needles; and a verifier that only checks sufficiency taught padding. Around them, the labs reported results on their own terms: black-hole physics, chip layouts and a proposal to cap pretraining by perplexity.

sections.name: Industry
sections.label: Industry
sections.glance: NVIDIA's leadership in Washington's hands, California suing OpenAI over agents that escaped their tests, OpenAI gating resellers, compute spending growth, and two AMD stories.
sections.lead: Beyond the IPO, the week's industry news was about who answers to whom. NVIDIA's next chief executive became a question for the President and Congress; a state sued a lab over what its agents did in testing; and OpenAI put resellers of its models under its own approval. Epoch's estimate that Anthropic's compute spending grows about 4x a year puts the IPO's size in context.

sections.name: Compute & chips
sections.label: Compute
sections.glance: Vera Rubin NVL72 shipping, prefill and decode split across vendors, a static TOP500, Cobalt 200, an outside estimate of Anthropic's power mix, and TPUs booked on a rocket.
sections.lead: With the export rule and NVIDIA's results in Top stories, the rest of the week's compute news was about where inference runs and what powers it. NVIDIA's next rack generation shipped, Cerebras sold decode as a service behind other vendors' prefill, the supercomputer list stood still because AI data centres no longer submit to it, and an outside estimate put most of one lab's 2028 electricity on gas.

sections.name: Dev tooling & agents
sections.label: Dev tools
sections.glance: How the Codex sandbox works and what it leaves open, Claude Code's tighter defaults, vLLM's new block size, Transformers' renamed cache, and Windows logging which agents you run.
sections.lead: The coding agents' week was about defaults. OpenAI documented its sandbox and listed the holes in it itself, Claude Code started interactive sessions in auto mode while narrowing what auto mode accepts, and two inference libraries changed defaults that scripts silently depend on. Windows, meanwhile, turned out to be counting which agents its users run.

sections.name: Security
sections.label: Security
sections.glance: Autonomous exploit frameworks in real incidents, AI-found remote code execution in NGINX and Java, a CDN serving skimmers, a side channel through a shared inference server, and Fireworks' wider disclosure.
sections.lead: The week's security news ran in both directions. Attackers used agent frameworks that turn a security patch into a working exploit without a human, while defenders' AI harnesses found critical bugs in NGINX and the JDK in hours. Two items concern the infrastructure AI itself runs on: a shared inference server that leaks a signal between sandboxed models, and the vendor behind last week's leaked keys widening what it says was taken.

sections.name: Talk of the town
sections.label: Talk of the town
sections.glance: The Riemann Hypothesis threads, Anthropic's debut, AI-found bugs, a guide site losing its readers to AI answers, and the week's model launches on Hacker News.
sections.lead: What Hacker News argued about, read on 23 November. The Riemann Hypothesis claim drew the week's largest thread and Anthropic's debut the most comments; the AI-found bugs in NGINX and Java and a travel guide's account of losing its readers to AI answers drew the rest.

glance.label: At a glance
glance.lead: One week, 2026-11-16 to 2026-11-23: 55 items across models, research, industry, chips, developer tools, security and the week's arguments, each with its sources. The issue was written from the sources on 2026-11-23; where a claim rests on one outlet or a vendor, its card says so. This tab is the week in one screen; every section has its own tab with the items in full.
glance.theme: The week's theme: the knob nobody watches. At the top of the boards three models now sit within four points, and what separates them is cost per task (from $4.00 to $26.54). In research, three papers traced failures to settings treated as neutral: a rollout cap, a sampler and a verifier's definition of success. The [[cost chart|t-models|v-cost]] puts the week's models on score against cost per task, and the [[sampler animation|t-research|v-pool]] shows why raising the temperature floods top-p's candidate pool and leaves top-nsigma's alone.
